newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny edges toward second Gulf landfall.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny edges toward second Gulf landfall.

text.p: Hurricane Danny lashed the U.S. coastline from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle with high winds and torrential rains on Saturday, as it crept towards a second landfall near Mobile.
At 8 a.m. CDT (1300 GMT), the National Weather Service said the eye of the storm was about 30 miles (48.3 km) southeast of Mobile and drifting slowly towards the northeast.
Tornado watches were in effect for the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southwestern Georgia.

A minimal hurricane, Danny was packing maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (121 kph). Forecasters expected the system to be downgraded quickly to tropical storm status as it came ashore and wind velocity died down.

Hurricane warnings remained in effect from Gulfport, Mississippi, to Apalachicola, Florida. But Danny remained small in stature as well as in strength, with maximum winds extending only 25 miles (40 km) from its centre.

Because of the storm's sluggish motion, however, punishing winds and rain pounded the southern Alabama coastline for hours Saturday, smashing beachfront properties, stripping away roofs and playing havoc with electrical and telephone service.
Eyewitnesses in the beachfront community of Gulf Shores, Alabama, said waves were breaking over the town's seawall as high winds swept flying debris into the streets.
Danny came ashore for the first time early Friday in Louisiana, between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River, before moving back into the Gulf on a lumbering northeasterly track.

The hurricane claimed at least two lives Friday as it veered toward its second landfall in as many days. An elderly man had a heart attack while securing his boat against rising waters in Pirate's Cove, Alabama. Another man was found dead in a swamped sailboat near Fort Morgan, Alabama.

High winds caused sporadic power outages throughout the region Friday. A sea-going tornado, known as a water spout, damaged boats and tore roofs off buildings in a marina near Orange Beach, Alabamma. No injuries were reported.

But officials said the biggest worry was flash-flooding near rivers, streams and saturated lowlands. Weather forecasts called for up to 20 inches (50 cm) of rain along the storm's track over the course of the weekend.
"There's going to be a lot of wind. But our primary concern is rainfall due to its slow movement," said David Eversole, who heads the National Weather Service office in Mobile.

Many coastal residents, long accustomed to more powerful storms, chose to ride out the hurricane and spent all day Friday loading up on batteries and other household goods or nailing sheets of plywood over their windows.
One Alabama resident spray-painted his boarded-up home with the defiant message, "Danny is a Wanna-be."

But others, including thousands of vacationers from the area's surrounding resorts, joined long lines at gas stations before venturing into a steady stream of traffic headed for inland hotels and Red Cross shelters.
"We're staying," said Vicki Bruce, a tourist from Lexington, Ky. "There's more danger getting hurt in a traffic jam than there is from this storm."
The governors of Mississippi and Alabama each declared a state of emergency Friday, while authorities in southern Alabama issued a voluntary evacuation order of low-lying coastal areas.
All but one of the 11 floating casinos moored along the Mississippi coastline kept their doors open to a trickle of diehard gamblers and tourists.
"It's a little slower than normal, but it's been consistent all day," observed Lori Hutzler, spokeswoman for the Isle Capri Casino in Biloxi, which is open 24 hours a day.
"Patrons went out to get their supplies and then came back to gamble," she said.
